547.title: Deeds without measure (Mishnah Peah 1:1)
547.hook: the morning service lists things with no limit: honoring parents, kindness, hospitality, visiting the sick
547.howItsDone: Many prayer books place the Mishnah Peah passage and the list from tractate Shabbat right after the blessings over Torah study, so that each morning begins with a little learning about kindness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, neshamah, the soul the morning prayer calls pure. Your line was the soul is pure. Today, a list read every morning, of things with no ceiling.

Almost everything in a life of practice has a size. So many minutes of prayer. So many words in a blessing. A tenth of the harvest. Rules like that are a gift: you know when you've done it. But early in the morning service, many prayer books include a passage that goes the other way. It names a handful of things and says: these have no measure. It's a short list, and it starts in a farmer's field.
screen: `EVERYTHING HAS A SIZE.` → `YOU KNOW WHEN YOU'RE DONE.` → `THESE HAVE NO MEASURE.`

segments.voice: The passage is the opening of the Mishnah, tractate Peah: these are things that have no measure. First, peah, the corner of the field. The Torah tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested for the poor and the stranger, and never says how big the corner should be. Then the first fruits, and the pilgrim's offering at the Temple. Then gemilut chasadim, acts of loving-kindness. Then the study of Torah. The rabbis later set a minimum for the corner, one sixtieth of the field, and no maximum. Then the prayer book adds a second list, from the Talmud, tractate Shabbat: things whose fruit you enjoy in this life, while the principal stays for the world to come. Honoring your father and mother. Acts of kindness. Taking in guests. Visiting the sick. Helping a bride marry. Walking with the dead to their burial. Making peace between people. And it ends: the study of Torah is equal to them all; one reading says that's because study leads to doing. Why so early in the morning, close to the blessings for waking? One reading: the morning has just given thanks for eyes and legs and strength, and here's what they're for. The Jerusalem Talmud adds a careful note: giving money has limits, so you don't impoverish yourself, but kindness done with your own body, your time, your presence, has none.

segments.voice: Let the list pass slowly: honoring a parent, a guest, someone sick, someone grieving, two people who aren't speaking. Notice which one brings a real name to mind, and stay with that person. Picture the smallest version of the deed: a call, a visit, a meal, a sentence that might make peace.

548.title: Learning before breakfast
548.hook: the day begins with a blessing over Torah, then a little study straight away
548.howItsDone: Jews who pray each morning say the blessings over the Torah early in the service, then immediately read a few short passages, often the priestly blessing, a mishnah and a passage of Talmud, so the blessing covers the day's study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, peah and the deeds without measure. Your line was no limit on kindness. Today, the blessing that comes just before that list.

A lot of mornings start by taking something in. Headlines. Messages. Somebody else's photos of somebody else's breakfast. Whatever comes first tends to set the weather for the morning. The Jewish prayer book has an opinion about what should come first. Very early, before the psalms, before the main prayers, before a single request, there's a blessing for studying Torah. Then, so the blessing isn't left hanging, a few lines to actually study, on the spot.
screen: `WHATEVER COMES FIRST SETS THE WEATHER.` → `A BLESSING FOR STUDY.` → `THEN STUDY, ON THE SPOT.`

segments.voice: The blessing comes from the Talmud, tractate Berakhot, where several rabbis each offer a wording, and the prayer book keeps more than one. The first thanks God who commanded us la'asok b'divrei Torah, to busy ourselves with the words of Torah. Not just to read, or to finish, but to be busy with it, the way you're busy with work. The next asks: make the words of Torah sweet in our mouths, and in the mouths of our children and their children. Sweet, the way honey is sweet. And the last is the one the Talmud calls the finest of blessings: who chose us and gave us the Torah. Then come a few lines of study, so the blessing has something to bless. In many prayer books, first the priestly blessing from the Book of Numbers, in the old Jewish translation: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee." Then the lists from yesterday, from the Mishnah and the Talmud. A verse of Torah, a mishnah, a passage of Talmud: a taste of each layer of the tradition. The Talmud takes this blessing seriously. In tractate Nedarim, it even suggests that when learned people's children didn't become learned, it was because their parents hadn't blessed the Torah first. Study, in this telling, isn't only information. It's a gift, received with thanks before you open it.

549.title: The binding in the morning
549.hook: many read the binding of Isaac each morning, asking for Abraham's devotion
549.howItsDone: Many Orthodox prayer books print the akedah (Genesis 22) near the start of the morning service with a request that follows it; some people say it privately each day, while other communities and prayer books leave it out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing over divrei Torah, with study right after it. Your line was learn something first. Today, one of the hardest stories in the Torah, read at the start of the day.

Genesis, chapter twenty-two. God tells Abraham to take his son Isaac up a mountain and offer him there. Abraham rises early, saddles the donkey, splits the wood. Father and son walk together for three days. On the mountain, Abraham builds an altar, binds his son, and lifts the knife. And an angel calls out and stops him. People have argued over this story for thousands of years; some of the most honest readers say it frightens them. And many Jews read it every morning, before breakfast.
screen: `GENESIS 22.` → `A FATHER, A SON, A KNIFE.` → `READ EVERY MORNING.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew it's the akedah, the binding, from the word for tying Isaac's hands and feet. The old Jewish translation opens the chapter: "God did prove Abraham." A test. When God calls, Abraham answers, "Here am I," and at the end, when the angel calls, he answers the same way. And the angel says: "Lay not thy hand upon the lad." Isaac isn't harmed. Why read it daily? The custom spread in the later Middle Ages, and the Shulchan Aruch, the sixteenth-century code of Jewish law, calls it good to say each morning. After it, many prayer books add a request, roughly: just as Abraham held back his compassion to do your will, so may your compassion hold back your anger from us. Abraham's devotion becomes something his children ask God to remember. The tradition calls this zechut avot, the merit of the ancestors: what the founders gave still counts for those who come after. Jews read this story many ways. Some see the height of faith: a person willing to give everything. Others stress the ending: the God of this story stops the knife, and many teachers have read it as a rejection of child sacrifice. Some live with the question and never settle it. Reading it every morning doesn't settle it either. It keeps the question, and the devotion, close.
screen: `AKEDAH: THE BINDING.` · `HERE AM I.` · `LAY NOT THY HAND UPON THE LAD.` · `ZECHUT AVOT: THE ANCESTORS' MERIT.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE BINDING.`

segments.voice: Think of someone, in your family, your history, your neighborhood, who gave something costly for what they believed or loved: a grandparent who crossed an ocean, a parent who worked two jobs, a friend who kept a promise when it hurt. Picture one moment of that devotion, and ask quietly: what of theirs am I still living on? If you pray, you can ask God to remember them.
Akedah. The binding — Genesis twenty-two's story of Isaac bound on the altar, read daily by many Jews, asking God to remember Abraham's devotion.
Your line: remember the binding. The question stays open, and the devotion stays close. Until tomorrow.

550.title: What are we?
550.hook: a humble prayer: what are we, what is our life, yet we are your people
550.howItsDone: In many prayer books, the passage beginning 'master of all worlds' and 'what are we' follows the morning blessings and leads into ashreinu, followed by the first line of the Shema, said early in the service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the akedah, the binding of Isaac, read each morning. Your line was remember the binding. Today, the prayer that comes right after it.

Stand at the edge of the ocean at night, or under a sky far from city lights, and problems start to look smaller. So does the one looking up. It can be humbling and freeing at once. A lot of ordinary life goes into feeling big: important, busy, needed. A few minutes into the morning, the prayer book does the opposite on purpose. Right after the story of Abraham, it asks a question you'd expect from someone staring at the stars. What are we?
screen: `UNDER A SKY FULL OF STARS.` → `PROBLEMS SHRINK. SO DOES THE ONE LOOKING.` → `WHAT ARE WE?`

segments.voice: The prayer begins: master of all worlds, we don't lay our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy. Then a string of short questions: what are we? What is our life? What is our kindness, our goodness, our strength? These opening questions are old. A version appears in the Talmud, tractate Yoma, among confessions said on Yom Kippur, and the morning prayer book borrowed them for every day. Then it piles on. Before you, the mighty are as nothing, the famous as if they'd never been, the wise as if they knew nothing. It even quotes Ecclesiastes: compared with the beasts, people have no advantage, for all is vanity. If it stopped there, it would be bleak. It doesn't. The next word is but. But we are your people, children of your covenant. Children of Abraham, whom you loved. The seed of Isaac, who was bound on the altar. The community of Jacob. And then it turns all the way around: therefore we are obligated to thank you. How fortunate we are, how good is our portion, how pleasant our lot. In Hebrew, ashreinu. Small, then loved, then grateful. It doesn't ask anyone to feel important. It sets smallness and being held side by side. A psalm asks it too: what is man, that God is mindful of him? The prayer's answer: not much, and dearly loved.

segments.voice: Picture the earth from far away, one blue dot, and you somewhere on it, too small to see, and let that take the weight off. Then bring to mind one person who loves you, or loved you once, and feel how big you are to them. Hold both pictures together; if you pray, you can say ashreinu, how fortunate we are.
Mah anu. What are we — the morning prayer's question, admitting how small people are, then turning: but we are your people, and how fortunate we are.
Your line: small, yet loved. The dot and the face, both true at once. Day five hundred fifty, done.

551.title: Words instead of bulls (Hosea 14:3)
551.hook: since the Temple fell, reading about the offerings stands in for them
551.howItsDone: Orthodox prayer books print the passages on the daily offering, the incense and the places of the offerings early in the morning service, and many people read them daily; other movements' prayer books shorten, recast or omit them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mah anu, the prayer that asks what are we, and answers: your people. Your line was small, yet loved. Today, a part of the morning that surprises people who find it.

Open a traditional prayer book to the early morning pages and you'll find instructions for animal offerings. The daily lamb, morning and evening. The recipe for the Temple incense, ingredient by ingredient. Where in the Temple each offering was slaughtered. Rome destroyed the Temple in Jerusalem long ago, and there hasn't been one since. So why are these pages in a book people carry to work on the train? The answer starts with a prophet, and a strange phrase: the bulls of our lips.
screen: `OFFERINGS IN THE PRAYER BOOK.` → `NO TEMPLE, NO ALTAR.` → `THE BULLS OF OUR LIPS.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew word is korbanot, offerings, from a root that means to come near. An offering was a way of drawing close. When the Temple stood, priests offered a lamb every morning and every evening, the tamid, the constant offering. Then it was gone. How do you draw near without an altar? The rabbis found an answer in the prophet Hosea. In the old Jewish translation: "Take with you words, and return unto the LORD." And a few lines on: "so will we render for bullocks the offering of our lips." Words, standing where the bulls once stood. The Talmud, in tractate Taanit, tells a story. Abraham asks God: when my children have no Temple, how will they be forgiven? God answers: I have already arranged for them the order of the offerings. Whenever they read it, I will count it as if they had brought them. So the prayer book prints the passages, and people read them. Communities treat these pages differently today. Orthodox prayer books keep them, and many add prayers for the Temple's rebuilding. Reform prayer books generally removed them. Conservative prayer books have often kept some readings while recasting the requests as remembrance. Across those differences runs Hosea's idea: words can carry what used to be carried on an altar.

segments.voice: Think of something you'd give, if giving were simple: an apology you owe, a thank you you never said, a promise you want to make. Shape the words slowly until they're true, then say them quietly, out loud. If you pray, you can offer them to God; if not, offer them to the person they belong to, in your mind.
Korbanot. Offerings, from the root for coming near. Since the Temple fell, the morning reading of them stands in their place.

552.title: Kaddish for the teachers
552.hook: a Kaddish praying for teachers, their students and their students' students
552.howItsDone: Kaddish d'Rabbanan is said in a minyan after a passage of rabbinic study, including in the morning service after the readings on the offerings; mourners often lead it, and the congregation answers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, korbanot, the offerings read in place of the altar. Your line was words instead of offerings. Today, the prayer that closes that section.

Every teacher had a teacher. The fourth-grade teacher who read aloud with all the voices learned it from someone. So did the coach, and the grandmother at the kitchen table. And who taught them? Somewhere back along that line is a stranger whose patience is still being passed along, though nobody remembers their name. Jewish prayer sets aside a moment for that whole invisible line. It comes right after a few minutes of study, and it's one of the forms of the Kaddish.
screen: `EVERY TEACHER HAD A TEACHER.` → `AND WHO TAUGHT THEM?` → `AN INVISIBLE LINE.`

segments.voice: The Kaddish is often thought of as the mourner's prayer. In fact it comes in several forms, and all share a core, in Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews in the age of the Talmud: may God's great name be made great and holy in the world. The congregation answers: may God's great name be blessed forever. The Kaddish d'Rabbanan, the Kaddish of the rabbis, is said after a group has studied rabbinic teaching together. In the morning service it comes at the end of yesterday's readings. And it adds a paragraph no other Kaddish has. It asks for blessing on Israel, and on the teachers, and on their students, and on all their students' students, and on everyone who studies Torah, here and in every place. It asks for peace, grace, kindness and compassion, long life, enough to live on, and help from heaven. Notice how far it reaches: not just my teacher, but students of students, across places and generations. Like every Kaddish, it's said only with a minyan, the quorum for communal prayer, and often mourners lead it. The Talmud, in tractate Sotah, says the world is held up by the response to the Kaddish said after study. Learning isn't treated as private. It ends with a prayer for everyone who carried it to you, and everyone you'll carry it to.

Then widen the picture: their teacher behind them, a line going back further than you can see, and forward to the people you've taught, even a little. If you pray, ask God's peace for the whole line; if not, simply wish it to them.
Kaddish d'Rabbanan. The Kaddish of the rabbis, said after study, with a paragraph for teachers and their students' students.

553.title: Warming up
553.hook: psalms before the main prayer, to prepare the heart
553.tomorrow: Blessed is the one who spoke
553.howItsDone: Pesukei d'Zimra is said each morning between the morning blessings and the Shema, opening with Baruch She'amar and closing with Yishtabach; on Shabbat and festivals more psalms are added, and many communities sing parts of it aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kaddish of the rabbis, for teachers and their students' students. That closes the morning blessings. Your line was pray for the teachers. Today, a new part of the prayer book.

No singer walks onstage cold. Backstage there are scales, humming, lip trills, the odd noises that loosen a voice. Runners jog before they run. Even a hard conversation goes better after a minute to breathe in the car. The body and the heart both need a ramp. The Jewish morning service has one built in. Before the Shema, before the standing prayer at its center, comes a long stretch of psalms and songs whose job, more or less, is to warm you up.
screen: `NO SINGER WALKS ON COLD.` → `THE HEART NEEDS A RAMP.` → `A STRETCH OF SONGS FIRST.`

segments.voice: It's called Pesukei d'Zimra, verses of song. It opens with a blessing, Baruch She'amar, closes with another, Yishtabach, and between them come psalms and passages of praise. The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, remembers that the early pious ones would wait an hour before praying, to direct their hearts. The Talmud adds a principle from Rabbi Simlai: always first set out the praise of God, and only then ask for anything. He learns it from Moses, who begins his plea with praise before asking to enter the land. And in tractate Shabbat, Rabbi Yose says: may my portion be among those who complete the praise every day. The Talmud explains he meant these verses of song, the psalms near the end of the Book of Psalms. So the order is deliberate. Thanks for waking, then a little study, then song, and only then the central prayers. Praise before asking. Some teachers love a play on the word zimra. The same three Hebrew letters can mean to sing and to prune, as you prune a vine. So the verses of song can be heard as verses of pruning, cutting away distractions so the prayer can grow. That's wordplay, not the word's history, but some find it fits the experience.
screen: `PESUKEI D'ZIMRA: VERSES OF SONG.` · `AN HOUR TO DIRECT THE HEART.` · `PRAISE FIRST, THEN ASK.` · `TO SING, AND TO PRUNE.` · then, large: `WARM UP THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Close your mouth and let a low hum start in your chest, any note, and feel it buzz in your ribs and face as it rises and falls like a slow tune with no words. If you know a melody from a prayer or a psalm, hum that; if not, anything gentle. Notice your breath lengthening and your shoulders softening.
Pesukei d'Zimra. Verses of song: the psalms and praise that warm the heart before the main prayer.

Your line: warm up the heart. A week of deeds without measure, learning first, the binding, what are we, words for offerings, a Kaddish for teachers, and verses of song. Day five hundred fifty-three, done.
